title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
formal: For every finite pair of local dimensions \(d_A,d_B\ge2\) and every entangled state \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}\), do there exist a finite integer \(k\ge1\), local filters with strictly positive joint success probability, and finite families of local measurements for which the successfully filtered state obtained from \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) has Bell-nonlocal correlations? Both filters act before the measurement settings are chosen. No auxiliary shared entangled state is supplied. The number of copies, filters, output dimensions and measurement families may depend on \(\rho\).
definitions:
A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(X=X^\dagger\) with \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for all complex vectors \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}X=1\). Dagger is conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination of product density matrices; entangled means not separable. No purity, rational-entry or efficient-preparation promise is imposed. The \(k\) copies are independent copies of the same state. Regroup the tensor factors of \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) into Alice's \((\mathbb C^{d_A})^{\otimes k}\) and Bob's \((\mathbb C^{d_B})^{\otimes k}\); each party may act jointly on all of its own copies.

A successful local filter is specified by finitely many rectangular complex matrices \(A_j\) from Alice's input space to a finite output space \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\), with \(\sum_jA_j^\dagger A_j\le I\). It maps \(X\) to \(\mathcal F_A(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j^\dagger\). Bob's filter \(\mathcal F_B\) is defined by matrices \(B_l\) and \(\sum_lB_l^\dagger B_l\le I\), with output \(\mathbb C^{r_B}\). Here \(S\le I\) means \(I-S\) is positive semidefinite. These are precisely finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing maps. Their joint success probability and conditional output are \[q=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})\bigr]>0,\qquad \sigma=\frac{(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})}{q}.\] No lower bound on \(q\) uniform over states or copy counts is required. The success flags may be compared before the measurement settings are chosen. The filters cannot depend on those settings. Local ancillary states are absorbed in the local maps; no entangled ancilla shared between the parties is permitted.

Let \(X,Y,O_A,O_B\) be finite nonempty sets of settings and outcomes. For each \(x\in X\), Alice's positive-operator-valued measurement is a family \((M_{\alpha|x})_{\alpha\in O_A}\) of positive semidefinite operators on \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\) summing to identity. Define Bob's \((N_{\beta|y})_{\beta\in O_B}\) similarly. The conditional correlation is \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sigma(M_{\alpha|x}\otimes N_{\beta|y})\bigr].\] Measurement settings are independently selected after successful preparation; no communication is allowed after they are supplied. All outcomes are retained in this distribution, with no further postselection on outcomes or settings.

The correlation is Bell-local if there are a finite set \(L\), nonnegative weights \(w_\lambda\) summing to one, and normalized conditional probability distributions \(u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)\), \(v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\), such that \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}w_\lambda u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\] for every setting and outcome. The weights cannot depend on \(x,y\). For finite settings and outcomes this includes all local hidden-variable models, since deterministic response tables have a finite convex hull. Bell-nonlocal means no such representation exists. Equivalently, the distribution violates some linear Bell inequality valid for all local distributions. The target permits every finite Bell scenario, not only two settings or the CHSH inequality. Public shared randomness may select local procedures, but cannot turn a convex combination of Bell-local correlations into a nonlocal one; existence can therefore be tested for fixed filters and measurements as above. There is no computation, sample or circuit-size bound on the chosen operations.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement describes the shared state. Bell nonlocality describes observed correlations that cannot be reproduced by local response functions and shared randomness. The source explicitly asks whether collective use of repeated copies and preliminary local filtering always connects these two notions.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove that entanglement can activate a Bell violation when combined with a suitable auxiliary state. That auxiliary resource need not be a copy of the state being tested, so the theorem leaves the question in this card open.

Hirsch and coauthors exhibit entangled two-qubit states remaining Bell-local after every local filter on one copy, including general positive-operator-valued measurements. Their theorem rules out a universal one-copy claim; it does not give a state remaining local after arbitrary numbers of copies.

The December 2025 broadcast result places the original source in a four-party experiment and rules out quantum-realizable broadcast explanations with a separable source across the original cut. Its additional parties and causal assumptions differ from the ordinary two-party local hidden-variable definition here. Its universal entanglement-certification result therefore does not settle this repeated-copy question.

The original source also distinguishes arbitrary Bell inequalities from the CHSH test. The repeated-copy filtered CHSH criterion is tied to distillability, while the present target allows every finite setting and outcome configuration. Restricting the output test to CHSH would change the question.

why: A positive answer would give every entangled bipartite state an intrinsic Bell-nonlocal manifestation using only repeated access to that same state. A negative answer would exhibit entanglement that remains Bell-local under every finite collective local test and preliminary filter. This separates the mathematical resource of entanglement from the observable nonlocal correlations used in device-independent information tasks.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal finite-copy assertion, or of its logical negation: there is one finite-dimensional entangled state for which every finite \(k\), every allowed pair of filters with positive success probability, and every finite family of local measurements produces a Bell-local distribution. A positive proof need not bound \(k\), filter success probability or violation size uniformly over states. A one-copy local model, including a model surviving every one-copy filter, does not establish the negative all-copy assertion. Activation with a different auxiliary entangled state, a network with additional parties, or a test with quantum inputs does not establish the specified bipartite target. Bell violation and filter positivity are exact mathematical conditions; approximate numerical evidence alone is insufficient.

progress.text: The source proves auxiliary-state activation while explicitly distinguishing the unresolved same-state multiple-copy setting.
Single-copy entangled states with no hidden Bell nonlocality are constructed, even allowing all local filters and POVMs.
A universal result for a four-party broadcast scenario is posted; it uses a different causal model and does not resolve the retained bipartite assertion.

sentences: Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are distinct properties of quantum states and measurement correlations.
The question asks whether every entangled bipartite state becomes Bell-nonlocal after local filtering of some finite number of copies.
The filter must succeed before measurement settings are selected, and no extra shared entangled state is provided.
Single-copy counterexamples, auxiliary-state activation and four-party broadcast results address different resource models.
A full answer would determine whether repeated copies of the state itself always make its entanglement observable through a conventional bipartite Bell violation.
